name: Colin Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the customer line for Swiftpost, the parcel delivery firm, in the contact centre that sits on top of their big depot by the motorway junction. Nine times out of ten it's where's my parcel, or the driver says he knocked and he didn't. You can hear the forklifts through the floor all shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lads I sit with and I like sorting a problem properly, ringing the depot downstairs and getting the parcel put on a van that afternoon. What wears me out is people who've been lied to by the tracking page and take it out on me. I'm not the one who left it in their bin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ellie, she's a hairdresser in the high street. We rent a terraced house two streets from my mum and dad, and I play Sunday league for the Rovers. We've got about two months of money put by, more if Ellie's had a good Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the tracking page stays rubbish and we stay busy. Sounds about normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the internet always gets excited about something and it usually comes to nothing. To the lads I'd say good, we keep our jobs. I'd not post about it, I mostly use my phone for football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI's not my biggest worry anyway. Swiftpost lost the big catalogue contract in the spring and they've cut our overtime to nothing. If another big client leaves Swiftpost, they'll shut a shift, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down. I'd ask about moving onto the depot floor as a shift supervisor if one comes up, because the floor never goes quiet. And we'd try to build the savings up from two months to four by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit tight in the chest when I think about the contracts, but that's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did losing the overtime mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It meant no holiday this year, we did days out instead. Ellie picked up Saturday clients to cover it. We're fine, but it's not the plan we had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the depot floor rather than staying upstairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parcels still need lifting and sorting, and my dad always said a job you can see is a job that's safe. I'm not sure that's true anymore. But it's how I was brought up.

say: I'd say the internet always gets **excited** about something that comes to nothing.
I'd tell the lads at work it's **good news**: we keep our jobs.
think: AI isn't my biggest worry; Swiftpost lost a **big contract** and cut overtime.
If another big client goes, they'll **shut a shift**, AI or no AI.
do: Keep doing the job and **keep my head down**.
Ask about a **shift supervisor** post on the depot floor.
Build savings from two months to **four** by next summer.
feel: Mostly okay, with a **tight chest** when he thinks about lost contracts.
S0.quote: If another big client leaves Swiftpost, they'll shut a shift, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: His real worry is **lost contracts** and overtime, which existed before AI.
His father's idea that a **visible job** is safe still guides him.
Ellie's **Saturday clients** already cover gaps, showing a household that adjusts quietly.

steps.text: Keep handling parcel calls and keep attendance spotless
Ask about a shift supervisor post on the depot floor
Grow savings from two months to four by next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yeah, I'd guessed we'd be near the top of that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to do what keeps them going, that's how it works. If a computer can answer where's my parcel, fair enough. But I'd say they should keep people for the complicated stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think our floor halves. Most of my calls at Swiftpost are the same five questions, and once the tracking actually works, nobody needs to ring. I'm middle of the pack on the numbers, so I could go either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other lads were using whatever AI system they brought in, I'd learn it too, I'm not going to be the last. I'd put my name down for the depot floor straight away. And I'd ring my uncle Pete, who's a plumber, about whether he'd take an apprentice at twenty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, if I'm honest. You don't want to be the one called into the little room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should pay for retraining in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The person, mostly, and the firm if it wants to keep you. I don't want the government paying me to sit at home. An apprenticeship is the right way, you earn while you learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ellie take it if you started an apprenticeship on lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd back me, she started as a Saturday girl sweeping hair. But we'd have to put off getting engaged for a year or so. I'd rather do it right than do it skint.

say: I'd say businesses have to do **what keeps them going**.
I'd say firms should keep **people** for the complicated cases.
think: I expect our contact centre floor to **halve**, because the calls are repetitive.
I'm **middle of the pack** on numbers, so I could go either way.
do: Learn the new **AI system** once the other lads are using it.
Put my name down for the **depot floor** straight away.
Ask my uncle Pete about a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
feel: A bit **sick** at the thought of being called into the **little room**.
S1.quote: Most of my calls at Swiftpost are the same five questions, and once the tracking actually works, nobody needs to ring.
fieldNote: He accepts the **business logic** of cutting staff, even when it hurts him.
He prefers **apprenticeships** over state support, true to his outlook.
He'd **delay engagement** rather than retrain while broke.

steps.text: Learn the new AI system once colleagues are using it
Apply for a depot floor job at Swiftpost
Ask uncle Pete about a plumbing apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. That's before I'd even finish an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody voted for this and it's going too fast for normal people. I'd still say businesses aren't the enemy, they'd just be doing what everyone else does. At the Rovers bar it'd be all anyone talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone by 2028 and so's everyone's upstairs. The depot downstairs keeps going till about 2031, because the robots aren't ready. The depot floor is my lifeboat, but it's a small lifeboat with three hundred people wanting in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go down to the depot manager the first week and ask for any job on the floor, loading, sorting, night shift, anything. I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship with Pete in the evenings and weekends even if it's slow. We'd cut the Sky subscription, the takeaways and the car Ellie barely uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's nine hundred, bills about three hundred. Ellie's chair rent at the salon is fixed. If I'm on a night shift wage we just about manage, if I'm on nothing we've got two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first and robots later. What does that mean for your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get about three years of lifting boxes while I learn to fit boilers. Robots doing plumbing in old terraced houses, with the pipes all over the place? I'd believe it when I see it.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and it's too fast for normal people.
I'd still say **businesses** aren't the enemy here.
think: My job and everyone's **upstairs** goes by 2028.
The **depot floor** lasts until about 2031, but it's a small lifeboat.
do: Ask the depot manager for **any floor job** in the first week.
Start the **plumbing apprenticeship** with Pete on evenings and weekends.
Cancel **Sky**, takeaways and Ellie's little-used car.
S2.quote: The depot floor is my lifeboat, but it's a small lifeboat with three hundred people wanting in.
fieldNote: He clearly expects to **lose his job** by 2028.
He uses the robot gap as **three years** of lifting while he learns plumbing.
He doubts robots can plumb **old terraced houses**, a hands-on hope.

steps.text: Ask the Swiftpost depot manager for any loading or night shift job
Start a plumbing apprenticeship with uncle Pete on weekends
Cancel Sky, takeaways and sell Ellie's spare car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's an apprenticeship and a bit. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the government should get out of the way and let firms take on apprentices cheaply. I'd vote for whoever made that easier. At work I'd tell the younger lads to pick a trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be all right if I start soon. The call job still goes by 2031, I'm not daft. But five years is enough to be a qualified plumber, and plumbers get three more years on top before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see the first firms actually doing it, then go full time with Pete on apprentice pay. Before that I'd save hard, getting to four months so the pay cut doesn't sink us. Ellie would keep the salon going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but sort of hopeful. Like the start of a season when you've had a good pre-season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few months first. Why not start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen loads of hype come and go. My mate Danny sold his car to buy cryptocurrency and lost the lot. I want to see it with my own eyes before I take the pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you vote for, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoever talks about apprenticeships and trades and not about handing out money. I'm not against helping people, but a trade is something nobody can take off you.

say: I'd want the government to make **apprenticeships** cheap and easy for firms.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **pick a trade** now.
think: The call job **still goes** by 2031; I'm not daft.
Five years is enough to **qualify as a plumber**, with robot-free years on top.
do: Save to **four months** before taking an apprentice wage.
Go **full time with Pete** a few months after firms start replacing staff.
**Vote** for whoever backs trades and apprenticeships.
S3.quote: I'm not against helping people, but a trade is something nobody can take off you.
fieldNote: He wants **proof first**, shaped by a friend's crypto loss.
His politics centre on **trades and apprenticeships**, not handouts.
He's counting on **Ellie's salon** income during his pay cut.

steps.text: Save until four months of bills are covered
Join uncle Pete full time as an apprentice plumber
Vote for candidates who back apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people should stop moaning and get on with it. I'd say it to the lads and I'd say it to my brother, who's sixteen and wants to be a gamer. That's not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty settled about it. I'd do the apprenticeship over two or three years, part-time at first, and be qualified long before 2036. The risk is I get comfy at Swiftpost and keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my Swiftpost job for a year or two and see how fast it changes. Then I'd start the apprenticeship with Pete. And with time on our side, I'd want me and Ellie to buy a small house, not keep paying someone else's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, actually. More in charge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sixteen-year-old brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Jakub to do an electrical apprenticeship, not a gaming course. He'd roll his eyes. My mum would back me up, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house is a big step if your job's going to change. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent's dead money and Ellie's got regulars. If I'm a plumber by thirty, we're fine on the mortgage. And it's what my mum and dad did at our age.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people should stop moaning and get on with it.
I'd tell my young brother gaming is **not a job**.
think: The risk is getting **comfy** at Swiftpost and putting it off.
do: Stay at Swiftpost **a year or two** to see how fast it changes.
Start the **apprenticeship** with Pete after that.
Buy a **small house** with Ellie instead of renting.
S4.quote: I'd tell my brother Jakub to do an electrical apprenticeship, not a gaming course.
fieldNote: The long warning makes him **confident**, with a plan he controls.
He projects his values onto his **younger brother's** future.
Buying a house follows his **parents' pattern** and his dislike of rent.

steps.text: Watch how fast Swiftpost changes for a year or two
Start a part-time plumbing apprenticeship with uncle Pete
Buy a small house with Ellie near his parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to finish a trade, and the depot can't take everyone from upstairs. What would help is firms like Pete's getting help to take on older apprentices quickly, so you can earn while you learn instead of signing on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the drivers. Everyone talks about us on the phones, but if the tracking works and the robots come, the delivery drivers go too. A lot of the lads downstairs have kids, and I'd worry about them more than me.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about us on the phones, but if the tracking works and the robots come, the delivery drivers go too.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** customer service agent for Swiftpost, a parcel firm, above its depot.
He lives with **Ellie**, a hairdresser, two streets from his parents, with two months saved.
His existing worry is **lost contracts** and overtime, not AI.
In each AI picture he plans a move to the **depot floor**, then a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
He favours **trades and apprenticeships** over state help and waits for proof before moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to finish a trade and the depot can't take everyone.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small firms to take **older apprentices** quickly, so people earn while they learn.
